frames.narration: The agent in a checkout-service process asks the rate controller for its settings. The service has a budget of 1% of a core, and the agent measures that one sample costs 250 microseconds, so it may sample 40 times per second.

For one minute the agent takes 2,400 samples at slightly random intervals. Many are identical, so it folds them into 310 distinct stacks, each with a hash id and a count. Only 15 of those stacks are new to the server.

The agent uploads 310 ids with counts, plus the full frames of the 15 new stacks, about 8 KB instead of the roughly 800 KB the raw samples would take. The gateway authenticates it and tags the data with the service, version, host and region.
The upload goes through the queue to a stack aggregator, which merges it with the uploads of the other 200 processes of this service and ignores a duplicate if the agent retried.
The new stacks contain addresses with a build id. The symbolizer finds the symbols for that build and turns each address into a function name, file and line, and keeps the answers in a cache.

The aggregator writes the minute to the profile store: each distinct stack once in the stack table, and small rows of series, minute, stack id and count in a compressed block, with the tags added to the index.
Later an engineer sees that checkout got slower after release v2.4. They ask for a diff of v2.3 against v2.4 over the same hour of the day.

The API builds one tree for each version and compares every node's share of its own total, so the different amount of traffic does not matter. render_json went from 15% to 40% of the samples, a 25 point increase, and its parent frames are coloured too. The engineer clicks the red box and finds the commit.
